I’ve been farming these fields in Quzhou for more than forty years, and I know this land like the back of my hand. My son and daughter both work in Handan city now, so it’s just me and my husband managing the plots. We have about six mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and I’m not about to gamble with some fancy new crop I’ve never grown before. Around here, the safe and sensible rotation is winter wheat followed by summer maize — that’s what the grain buyers want, that’s what the machinery service teams know how to harvest, and that’s what our soil and water can handle.

For the wheat, I’ll sow an improved variety — probably something like Jimai 22 or Luyuan 502 — in late October after rotary tillage. I learned long ago that good tillage before wheat helps the roots establish before the cold sets in. I’ll put down a basal compound fertilizer and topdress with urea at green-up and jointing; all told, I aim for about twenty-two kilograms of nitrogen, eight of phosphorus, and six of potassium per mu. Water is getting tighter every year, so I’ll irrigate four times: once before winter to protect against freeze, and three more in spring when the wheat is thirsty at the critical stages. I’ll spray herbicide once and keep an eye out for aphids and rust, so probably three pesticide applications in total. If the weather cooperates, I should get around 520 kg per mu.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I’ll plant summer maize with a hybrid seed — Denghai 605 or similar — using no-tillage direct seeding into the wheat stubble. There’s no time to waste between crops, and no-tillage saves fuel, labor, and moisture. Maize needs less irrigation than wheat here; two good waterings — one to help establishment and another at the large-trumpet stage — should be enough if the summer rains aren’t too stingy. I’ll fertilize at sowing and side-dress at the right time, targeting about twenty kilograms of nitrogen, six of phosphorus, and five of potassium per mu. I’ll watch for corn borer and weeds, so three pesticide applications again. With a decent summer, that maize should yield about 580 kg per mu.

I also keep a small home garden by the courtyard with cabbage, scallions, and spinach for our own table, but that’s just for eating, not for selling. The wheat and maize are what pay for our medicine, electricity, and my granddaughter’s school fees. I’m sticking with what works.
